Part Six · Safety

Chapter Twenty

Safety: Protect People First

A home can be cleared, arranged, and spotless and still hold every danger it started with, because tidy and safe are different questions. The fourth S turns from the state of the room to the people in it: look at the home through one new question, could this hurt someone, and fix what could hurt someone worst and soonest, first.

Stand in the home you have built across this book and look at it with plain pride. It is cleared of what did not belong. Everything that stayed has a place, and the places make sense, and they explain themselves. It is clean, and it stays clean, on fifteen minutes a day. By every measure this book has given you, it is finished, and it is good. And it could still send someone to the hospital tonight.

Not because you did anything wrong. Because nothing you have done so far was ever aimed at that. Sort asked whether a thing belonged. Straighten asked where it should live. Shine asked whether it was clean and what its condition was telling you. Three good questions, and not one of them is the question that notices the rug curling at the top of the stairs, or the medicine sitting at a toddler's eye level, or the smoke alarm that has been quietly dead since its battery gave out last spring. Those things were never messy, never misplaced, never dirty. They passed every test the first three S's could give, and they were dangerous the whole time.

That is why there is a fourth S, and why it is not an afterthought but a turn. For nineteen chapters this book has been about the state of the room. Safety is about the people in it, which is a different thing entirely and, when the two ever compete, the more important one. A cluttered counter is an annoyance. A cabinet a child can open is a catastrophe waiting for a quiet afternoon. This chapter teaches you to see the difference, to look at your finished home through one new question, and to act on what you find in the order that protects people first. It is the most important S in the book, and it asks the least tidying of any of them.

In this chapter

  • See why a clean, arranged, well-kept home can still be genuinely dangerous.
  • Understand why safety is its own S, and why it comes before tidiness and efficiency.
  • Look at your home through the safety lens: the question could this hurt someone.
  • Protect people first by ranking hazards by harm and fixing the worst and soonest ones first.
  • Make a first safety pass, and handle a few real dangers today so you can stop worrying about them.

The reframeA Clean Home Is Not a Safe Home

Let me say plainly the thing this whole part turns on, because it runs against a feeling most of us carry without examining it.

A clean home is not a safe home. Sort, Straighten, and Shine asked whether a thing belonged, where it lived, and whether it was clean. None of them asked whether it could hurt someone, so a home can be cleared, arranged, and spotless and still hold every danger it started with. Safety is the question the first three S's never ask.

We tend to feel that a tidy home is a safe one, that order and cleanliness add up to protection, and it is a comforting feeling and it is not true. Tidiness and safety overlap here and there, a cleared walkway is both tidy and safer, but they are not the same thing, and where they part ways the gap can be dangerous precisely because it is invisible. The most immaculate kitchen in the world is not made one bit safer by its gleam if the pan handles turn out over the edge of the stove where a child can reach them. The danger and the cleanliness are simply unrelated, and a home can score perfectly on one while failing quietly on the other.

This is worth sitting with, because it is the reason the fourth S has to exist as its own step rather than living inside the others. If cleaning made a home safe, we would not need to talk about safety separately; it would come free with Shine. It does not come free. Safety is a separate question that has to be asked on purpose, because the home will never raise it for you. A hazard does not announce itself the way a mess does. It sits there, tidy and patient, until the day it does not.

The plus oneWhy Safety Is Its Own S

There is a small piece of history here that is worth knowing, because it is the story of the very "plus one" that makes this book about six S's and not five.

The method began with five S's. When it spread beyond the factory floor, people saw that not one of the five, on its own, guaranteed the people in the space were safe, so safety was added as its own S, the plus one in what was first called 5S+1. It was not that the others ignored safety. It was that something this important should never be left to chance, and making it a step of its own is a way of refusing to assume it.

The original method, born on the factory floors of Toyota, had five steps, and safety was meant to run through all of them. And it did, and it does; a sorted, arranged, clean workspace really is a safer one. But as the method spread and people lived with it, they noticed that "safety runs through everything" has a quiet failure mode: what belongs to everything can end up owned by no one, exactly the trap you met with the cleaning in Chapter 17. Something that matters as much as whether people get hurt cannot be left as a happy side effect of the other steps. So it was pulled out and named, given its own S, made a thing you do on purpose rather than a thing you hope falls out of the rest.

That is the whole reason this S comes with the word first in its title. It is not first in sequence; you did it fourth, after the home was cleared and arranged and clean, and that order is fine. It is first in priority. When a safety fix and a tidiness improvement and an efficiency tweak all want your Saturday, safety wins, every time, without a debate, because the downside on the other two is inconvenience and the downside on safety is somebody you love getting hurt. Protecting people is not one item on the list competing with the others. It sits above the list.

The new questionThe Safety Lens

So how do you see what you have been walking past for years? You change the question. For three parts of this book you have looked at your home asking, in various forms, is this in order. Now you look at the same home asking something else entirely.

Ask not whether it is tidy, but whether it could hurt someone.

That single swapped question is the whole tool, and it is more powerful than it sounds, because a question decides what you are able to see. Ask "is this tidy?" and your eye slides over the dead smoke alarm, which is, after all, perfectly tidy. Ask "could this hurt someone?" and the same smoke alarm lights up like a warning, because now you are looking for the right thing. The professionals call this developing safety consciousness, which sounds grand and means something simple: teaching your eye a new question until asking it becomes automatic. What you are building is not fear. It is a habit of noticing.

And it helps to know exactly what you are noticing, so here is the plain definition, straight from the method and shrunk to fit a home.

Hazard

A hazard is any thing or situation in a home that could hurt someone: the loose rug, the pills within reach, the dead smoke alarm, the wobbling shelf. It does not have to look like a mess. Most hazards are perfectly tidy.

Read that last line twice, because it is the thing people miss. We picture hazards as obvious, dramatic, dirty, a frayed wire throwing sparks, a spill on the floor. A few are. But most of the real dangers in a home are quiet and orderly and have been sitting in plain sight so long that they have become furniture to you. The lens is how you make them visible again, by asking, of everything your eye has stopped seeing, the one question that turns furniture back into a hazard.

TriageProtect People First

Ask the safety question honestly of a whole home and you will find more than you expected, and that can tip quickly from useful into overwhelming. The answer to overwhelming is not to look away; it is to put the findings in order, because not all hazards are equal and they are not meant to be treated as if they were.

Protect people first: fix what could hurt someone worst and soonest, before anything else.

Rank what you find by two plain measures: how badly it could hurt someone, and how soon or how likely it is to. A dead smoke alarm and a bottle of pills a small child can open score high on both, they could cause terrible harm and the chance is real and present, so they go to the very top and they get fixed today. A bannister that is slightly loose but holds fine could matter someday and is not going to fail this week, so it waits its turn. This is not being casual about the bannister. It is refusing to let the bannister, and forty other small things, crowd out the two that could actually hurt someone this afternoon. Safety is triage, and triage means the worst first, on purpose, without apology.

And here is why you act on the top of that list now rather than someday, and it comes straight from a pattern safety workers have watched for a century.

Safety work has long noticed a pattern, sometimes called Heinrich's Principle: a large pile of small hazards produces mostly near misses and minor hurts, and, every so often, out of the same pile, one serious injury. You can rarely tell in advance which hazard is the dangerous one. That is exactly why you do not wait for the serious injury to act: you remove the hazards while they are still only near misses, because the whole aim is to never find out which one it was.

That is the quiet logic under "protect people first." You are not fixing the smoke alarm because you expect a fire tonight; you almost certainly will not have one. You are fixing it because you cannot know which of a home's small dangers is the one that will matter, and the cost of removing them while they are harmless is so low, and the cost of guessing wrong so high, that there is nothing to weigh. Handle the worst ones now, while they are still just items on a list, and the day you would have found out which one was real simply never comes.

The heart of itSafety Is Love, Not Fear

If this chapter has started a small knot of anxiety in you, a sense that your home is a minefield and you have been negligent, stop and read this next part carefully, because it is the heart of how the fourth S is meant to feel.

None of this is about living afraid or wrapping your home in foam. It is the opposite. You handle the few real dangers plainly, once, so that you can stop carrying them around as worry. Safety done well is quiet: it is what lets a parent breathe out, because the things that could go wrong have been dealt with instead of feared.

The goal of safety is not vigilance. Vigilance is exhausting and it does not scale; you cannot watch everything forever, and the attempt just turns a home into a place of low, constant dread. The goal is the opposite of vigilance: it is to deal with the real dangers so thoroughly, and so early, that you no longer have to watch for them at all. You latch the cabinet once, and then you never again have to track where the toddler is in relation to the bleach, because the bleach is handled. You put the working battery in the alarm, and then the whole category of "what if there's a fire and we don't wake up" simply closes. Every hazard you remove is not just a harm prevented; it is a worry you get to set down and never pick up again.

That is why safety, of all the S's, is the one most rooted in love rather than order. You are not tidying here. You are quietly, unglamorously making sure the people you live with come to no harm in the place that is supposed to be their safest, and then, having made sure, you get to relax inside it. A safe home is not a fearful one. It is the one where you have already done the worrying, once, with your hands, so you do not have to keep doing it with your mind.

AppliedA First Safety Pass

So make a start, today, and keep it small, because protecting people first means the first pass is not a thorough hunt; it is the worst few things, handled now. Take the lens for a slow walk through the home you know so well you have stopped seeing it, and let it show you the dangers hiding in plain sight.

You will find them quickly once you are asking. The smoke alarm you cannot remember ever testing: press the button, and if it is silent, a new battery goes in before you do anything else on this list, because nothing else you find will matter as much. The cupboard under the sink, tidy and ordinary, full of cleaning bottles at the exact height of a small child: everything in it that could poison someone goes up high or behind a latch today. The rug at the top of the stairs that has always slid a little: a strip of grip tape underneath, or the rug gone, because a fall down a staircase is precisely the worst-and-soonest kind of hazard. Even the launch pad, that first small victory by the door, gets the new question: is anything heavy stored where it could fall on someone, is a charging cord strung where a foot could catch it, is there anything at knee height a crawling child could reach. Fix what the lens finds at the top of the list, and leave the rest for the thorough pass that is coming.

Notice what that walk was and was not. It was not a deep clean and it was not a tidy; the home was already both. Nothing moved for the sake of order. A few things moved, or got latched, or got a fresh battery, purely because they could hurt someone, and now they cannot. That is Safety in its smallest complete form: one lens, one walk, the worst dangers handled first, and a handful of the ways your home could have hurt someone quietly closed off for good.

Quick Win

Walk one room and find the single thing most likely to seriously hurt someone, the unlatched medicine, the rug that slides at the top of the stairs, the smoke alarm with a dead battery, and fix that one thing today. You just protected people first.

6S Tip

Get down to a child's height and look. Most of the worst home hazards, low cupboards, dangling cords, small swallowable things, sit in a band of space adults never look at because they never live there. A lot of danger is at knee height.

The stepThe Needle Takes Its First Safety Step

Go and look at the friction meter, because it moves again, and it moves for a reason it has never moved for before.

Every step until now, the needle traveled because the home got less cluttered, better arranged, or cleaner: because the daily friction of living there went down. This time nothing about the daily friction changed at all. The counters are no tidier than they were this morning; the home is no cleaner. And yet the needle steps toward calm, because a few real dangers that were in this home are now gone, and removing the chance of harm is the deepest kind of friction there is. It is not the friction you feel every day. It is the friction of the worst day, the one you are keeping from ever arriving, and taking that away moves the needle more honestly than any amount of tidying.

Protect people first.

The step is real and, you will notice, it is small, and both of those are true on purpose. Small, because the earlier S's already removed most of what this meter measures; the home was already close to calm, so what remains is not big friction to clear but important things to lock down, and safety, standards, and staying power move the needle in smaller, quieter increments than the first sweep of clearing and arranging did. Real, because a hazard removed is a genuine and permanent gain, worth every millimetre it earns. Chapter 19's Shine-complete milestone is the passed marker just behind the live needle now; the goal, out on the calm side, is still ahead, because Safety has barely begun, with a thorough hazard hunt and a whole layer of lasting safety still to come, and Standardize and Sustain beyond them. The needle moved for the best of reasons today. It also has real distance left, and both are true at once.

Family Challenge

Ask everyone, including the children, to point out one thing in the home they think could hurt someone. Children notice hazards adults have stopped seeing, and being asked makes them safer. Fix the worst one together.

In closingSafety Has Only Begun

You changed the question, and that changes everything that follows. You looked at a finished, cared-for home through the one lens the first three S's do not carry, and it showed you a handful of ways the place could hurt the people in it. You put those findings in order by harm, you handled the worst ones today, and, doing it, you traded a little vague background worry for the solid quiet of a few real dangers dealt with. That is the fourth S in a single pass: not a tidier home, a safer one.

What you have not done is the thorough part, and that is deliberate, because a first pass catches the dangers that are obvious once you are finally looking, and it will walk right past the ones that are not. The medicine you thought of is handled; the button battery in the old remote that a toddler could swallow, the space heater too close to the curtain, the extension cord run under the rug where it can overheat, those take a calmer, more systematic search than a first walk gives. That search is the next chapter. And past it lies the work of making safety not a one-time sweep but a lasting part of how the household lives, which is the chapter after. For now, hold on to the lens, because it works in any room, on any day: not is it tidy, but could it hurt someone.

Common Mistake

Treating every hazard as equal and trying to fix them all at once, so you fix none. Safety is triage, not a spreadsheet. The dead smoke alarm cannot wait; the slightly loose bannister can. Rank by harm, and start at the top.

One Idea to Keep

Protect people first. Walk the home asking not whether it is tidy but whether it could hurt someone, fix what could hurt someone worst and soonest before anything else, and you trade a low hum of worry for the quiet of a home whose real dangers have been handled.

Next

Chapter 21 · Find and Remove Hazards. You have the lens and you have handled the worst few dangers; now Safety gets thorough. The next chapter is a calm, room-by-room search for the hazards a first pass always misses, so the whole home, not just its most obvious dangers, is made safe.

↑ Contents

Part Six · Safety

Chapter Twenty-One

Find and Remove Hazards

A first pass catches the dangers that are obvious the moment you finally look, and walks straight past the rest. This chapter makes Safety thorough: a calm, room-by-room hunt that carries the same short set of questions into every space, finds the hazards hiding in plain sight, and removes each one the moment it is found. Find it, and fix it now.

Last chapter you took the safety lens for a first walk through your home, and it showed you a handful of real dangers, and you handled them. The smoke alarm has a fresh battery. The cleaning bottles are up high or behind a latch. The rug at the top of the stairs no longer slides. If you did that, you have already done something that matters, and you felt the particular relief of it, the sense of a worry set down.

Here is the honest next thing, and it is not said to take that relief away but to finish the job it started. The dangers you found on that first pass were the obvious ones. They were the hazards that light up the instant you finally ask the safety question, because they are the ones we already half-know about: the alarm we have been meaning to check, the bottles we always meant to move. And the obvious hazards, it turns out, are the minority. Most of what can quietly hurt someone in a home is not obvious at all. It is camouflaged, sitting in plain sight, wearing the disguise of a completely ordinary object, and it will survive any number of quick glances precisely because a glance is not built to catch it.

So this chapter is the search the first pass was not. It is a calm, thorough, room-by-room hunt for the hazards that hide, and, just as much, it is the discipline of removing each one the moment you find it. A first pass is a glance across a finished home. A hunt is a walk through it with a method and a roll of tape, room by room, missing nothing on purpose. That is how you get from a home whose worst dangers are handled to a home that is, all the way through, genuinely safe.

In this chapter

  • See why the obvious hazards are the few, and the hidden ones the many.
  • Run a hazard hunt: a systematic, room-by-room search that leaves nothing to memory.
  • Carry the same five safety questions into every room, so the search is complete.
  • Recognize the camouflaged hazards a first pass always walks past.
  • Remove each hazard the moment you find it, because a danger is only handled once it is gone.

Why thoroughFrom a Glance to a Search

The whole reason for this chapter is a simple, slightly uncomfortable fact about how we see our own homes.

A first pass finds the dangers that are obvious the moment you look. A hunt finds the ones that never will be. Most of what can quietly hurt a person at home lives in the second group.

A first pass works by noticing what stands out, and the hazards that stand out are a small and particular set: the ones dramatic enough, or familiar enough, to catch the eye of someone doing a quick scan. That is genuinely worth doing, and it is why the last chapter came first. But the eye doing a quick scan is the same eye that has looked at this room ten thousand times, and it has long since stopped seeing most of what is in it. The cord that has run under the rug for three years is not going to announce itself now. The bookcase that has never once fallen reads, to a glance, as furniture, not as a tall heavy thing that is not attached to anything.

This is not a failure of attention or of care. It is just how familiarity works: the things we live with become invisible to us, and the dangerous ones become invisible right along with the harmless ones. Which means the only reliable way to find the hidden hazards is to stop relying on what catches your eye and start running a method instead. You do not wait to notice a hazard. You go looking for it, deliberately, in every room, asking the same questions you would ask in a room you had never seen before. The point of a hunt is that it finds what a glance cannot, because it does not depend on the thing being obvious. It depends only on your walking the whole home and asking.

The methodThe Hazard Hunt

So here is the tool, and it is less a gadget than a habit of moving through the house.

The hazard hunt

A hazard hunt is a calm, systematic walk through the whole home, one room at a time, asking the same short set of safety questions in every space and removing each hazard you find before you move on. Where a first pass catches what is obvious, the hunt is built to catch what is hidden.

Three things make it a hunt rather than another glance. It is systematic: you go room by room, in an order, so that no space is skipped because you happened not to think of it. It is fixed: you carry the same short list of questions into every room, so the search does not depend on what you happen to remember to look for on a given day. And it ends in action: you fix what you find before you leave the room, so that finding a hazard and removing it are one motion, not two. The method is almost aggressively boring, and that is the point. Boring is what thorough looks like.

Go room by room. Ask the same few questions in each. Fix what you find before you leave.

What the hunt is really designed to defeat is camouflage, because that is what hides the dangerous ones.

The dangerous thing is rarely the ugly one. It is the ordinary object doing a second, quiet job you never gave it: the lamp cord that is also a tripwire, the old remote that is also a battery a small child can reach, the space heater that is also a flame a foot from the curtain.

None of those objects looks like a hazard, because none of them is only a hazard. The lamp is a lamp; it is a good lamp; it just also happens to have a cord strung across the place people walk. The remote is a remote; it also holds a small round battery that, swallowed, does real harm, behind a cover a determined toddler can open. You are not hunting for junk or mess, which the earlier S's already cleared. You are hunting for ordinary, tidy, useful things that are quietly doing a dangerous second job, and the only way to catch them at it is to ask.

The toolThe Five Questions

Here is the short list you carry into every room. It comes, home-scaled, from the questions the method has always asked on a safety walk, and it is deliberately small enough to hold in your head.

In every room, ask:

  1. Could someone fall here?
  2. Could something here burn, or catch fire?
  3. Could something here poison, choke, or strangle?
  4. Could something here fall, cut, or crush?
  5. Could water and electricity meet?

Five questions, and between them they catch the great majority of what hurts people at home. Each one is a different lens, and each finds a different family of hidden hazard.

Could someone fall looks down and looks at the edges: the rug that slides, the tread with a stray shoe on it, the wet patch by the tub, the top of the stairs, the small child near the low window. Falls are the most common serious home injury and the most walked-past, because floors and stairs are exactly what a familiar eye stops seeing.

Could something burn, or catch fire looks for heat too near things that burn and for electricity asked to do too much: the heater a foot from the curtain, the candle under the shelf, the outlet with a nest of plugs feeding a nest of cords, the lint packed in the dryer trap, the pan left where a sleeve can catch it.

Could something poison, choke, or strangle looks low, and looks for the small and the looped: the cleaning sprays and medicines within a child's reach, the button batteries and coins and small parts on the floor, the looped blind or curtain cord at a child's height, the plastic bag left where small hands find it.

Could something fall, cut, or crush looks up and looks at what is heavy and free: the tall bookcase or dresser not anchored to the wall, which can tip when a child climbs it, the heavy box on the top shelf, the knives within reach of the counter's edge, the drawer that slides all the way out.

Could water and electricity meet looks in the wet rooms: the hairdryer or radio near the filled basin, the frayed cord by the sink, the outlet without protection near water. Where those two meet, a small accident becomes a serious one.

You do not need to memorize categories of hazard or become an inspector. You need five plain questions and the willingness to ask all five in every room, and when the answer to any of them is yes, to do the one thing the answer asks for.

The ruleFind It, and Fix It Now

There is a strong temptation, once you start finding things, to do the finding now and the fixing later: to walk the whole home with a notepad, write down every hazard, and come back to deal with them when you have time. Resist it, because that is the one move that quietly turns a hazard hunt back into a hazard museum.

A hazard you have found but not fixed is not handled. It is scheduled. And a hazard on a schedule is still a hazard, still able to hurt someone on any ordinary day before its turn comes up. The only safe place for a danger is gone.

The notepad feels like progress, and it is not, because a written-down hazard is exactly as dangerous as an un-written-down one. The child does not know the button battery is on your list. The fire does not check whether you meant to move the heater this weekend. Between finding a danger and removing it there is a gap, and everything bad that a hazard can do, it can do in that gap. So you close the gap to nothing: you fix each hazard the moment you find it, before you move on. This is the source's oldest safety instruction, "address all possible safety issues immediately", and it is the whole reason the hunt ends in action rather than in a list. Carry a roll of grip tape, a few cabinet latches, and an empty box, not a notepad, and let finding and fixing be one motion.

Most of what you find will yield to that, because most home hazards are cheap and quick to remove: a cord tucked out of the walkway, a bottle moved to a high shelf, a latch fitted, a rug taped, a pot handle turned in, a heavy thing brought down. The fix is usually smaller than the worry was. Now and then you will meet a hazard whose full fix is genuinely bigger than "now", a bookcase that needs a bracket you do not have, a step that needs rebuilding. The rule still holds, with a small honest amendment: make it safe now, even if you cannot make it finished now. Move the climbing-height toys off the unanchored bookcase today, and buy the bracket this week. Reduce the danger to near nothing immediately, and schedule only the part that truly cannot be done on the spot. What you never do is walk away from a live hazard having changed nothing but your to-do list.

Quick Win

Pick one room and give it a full hunt right now. Ask the five questions, and fix everything you can in ten minutes before you walk out: the cord tucked away, the pills moved up high, the rug taped down, the heavy thing brought off the top shelf. One room, thoroughly safe, today.

6S Tip

Hunt every room twice, once standing and once low. Crouch to a small child's height and look again: the outlet at ankle level, the tablecloth a toddler can pull, the cleaning spray under the sink, the wobbling table leg. A whole layer of hazards lives in the band of space adults never occupy.

Worked throughA Room-by-Room Hunt

Let me walk it with you, the way you would actually do it, room by room, so you can see how ordinary the finds are and how quickly each one closes.

Start in the kitchen, because it holds more of all five kinds of hazard than any other room. Could someone fall: the rug by the sink is fine, but there is a slick spot where the dishwasher leaks a little, worth a look. Could something burn: a pot handle is turned out over the front edge of the stove where a passing hip or a reaching child could catch it, so you turn it in, a two-second fix you will now do by reflex forever. Could something poison or choke: the sprays under the sink are behind the latch you fitted last chapter, good, but a butane lighter sits in an open drawer at child height, and it goes up high. Could something fall or cut: the knives live in a block, but pushed to the very edge of the counter, so you slide them back. Could water and electricity meet: nothing by the sink, good. Four small fixes, one room, a few minutes.

The bathroom is quick and high-value. The hairdryer is plugged in beside the filled-at-bath-time basin, so it gets unplugged and moved to a drawer away from the water. The medicines are up, from last chapter. The bath mat has no grip, so it gets a grip pad or a wash-and-replace with one that does. A nightlight goes in, because most bathroom falls happen in the dark.

The living room is where camouflage lives. The tall bookcase has stood free of the wall for years and never fallen, and it is exactly the kind of tall, heavy, unanchored thing a climbing toddler can bring down on themselves, so it gets a simple anti-tip strap to the wall today. On the sofa arm is the old remote whose battery cover has gone loose, holding a button battery a small child could reach and swallow, so a strip of tape holds the cover shut until you replace it. And there, at last, is the lamp cord Chapter 20 promised would take a real hunt to catch: run under the edge of the rug, where it is both a thing to trip on and a wire being slowly crushed and heated where you cannot see it. It comes out from under the rug and gets routed along the wall.

The stairs and hall want two of the questions. Could someone fall: the treads are clear, but the hall runner has curled at one end, so it gets tacked flat, and a nightlight goes in at the top of the stairs. The child's room wants the poison-choke-strangle question most: the blind cord hangs in a loop at exactly a toddler's height, one of the quietest serious hazards in any home, so it gets wound up onto a cleat well out of reach, and the small parts and coins on the low shelf go up.

And the launch pad, your first small victory by the door, gets the hunt too, and pays off the last of Chapter 20's teasers. The little space heater you run on cold mornings sits a foot from the curtain, a flame beside a fabric, so it moves to a clear spot and gets a rule about the curtain. The charging cords are tucked so no foot catches them. Nothing here needed a deep clean or a rearrange; it was already sorted and arranged and clean. It just, in a handful of small ways, could have hurt someone, and now, room by room, it cannot.

Family Challenge

Turn the hunt into a game. Give each person a room and the five questions and send everyone off to find hazards at once, and the younger the sharper for the low ones. Then come back together and fix the worst finds as a team. A home searched by five pairs of eyes misses far less than one.

The stepThe Needle Takes Another Safety Step

Go and look at the friction meter, because it has moved again, and this time it moved for the same reason as last time, only more so.

The first Safety step, last chapter, came from removing a few real dangers on a first pass. This step comes from removing a whole home's worth, room by room, all the hidden ones a first pass could never reach. And again, notice what did not change: nothing got cleaner, nothing got tidier, no object found a better home. The daily friction of living here is exactly what it was this morning. What dropped, again, is the home's exposure to harm, and that is the deepest kind of friction there is, not the friction you feel every day but the friction of the worst day, the one you are keeping from ever arriving. A roomful of quiet dangers is simply gone, so the needle steps a little further toward calm.

Find it, and fix it now.

The step is a touch larger than the first one, because a thorough hunt clears more than a first glance did, and it is still, in absolute terms, a measured one, and both of those are honest. Larger, because you did more: you did not handle the obvious few, you searched the whole home and removed the hidden many. Measured, because the earlier S's already cleared the bulk of what this meter tracks, and safety moves it in the smaller, quieter increments of things locked down rather than things swept out. Chapter 20's first Safety step is the dashed ghost just behind the live needle now; Chapter 19's Shine-complete milestone sits further back as a passed marker; and the goal, out on the calm side, is still ahead. It is still ahead because Safety is not finished when the hazards are gone. It is finished when the home is made to keep itself safe, which is one more chapter, and Standardize and Sustain follow that. The needle moved for the best of reasons again, and it still has real distance to go, and both are true at once.

In closingSafety, Made Thorough

You carried five plain questions through the whole home, one room at a time, and you removed what they found before you left each room. That is the fourth S made thorough: not a first pass on the obvious dangers, but a complete sweep that reached the hidden ones, the button battery and the blind cord and the unanchored bookcase and the heater by the curtain, the hazards that would have survived any number of glances because they were wearing the disguise of ordinary things.

What is left is not more hazards to find, at least not today; it is the question of tomorrow. A hunt makes a home safe as of the day you run it, and homes do not hold still. New things come in, batteries die, a bracket loosens, a child grows tall enough to reach a shelf that was safe last month. Making safety survive that, turning a one-time sweep into a home that stays safe, and preparing calmly for the few emergencies you cannot prevent, is a different kind of work, and it is the next chapter, the one that completes the fourth S. For now, you have done the thing that had to come first: you found the dangers that were already here, and you removed them. Hold on to the five questions, because they work in any room, on any day, and a home you can hunt is a home you can keep safe.

Common Mistake

Walking the home with a notepad, listing hazards to deal with later, and calling that safety. The list is not the fix. Every danger you write down and leave in place is still live. Carry a roll of tape and a box instead of a notepad, and fix as you find.

One Idea to Keep

Go room by room, and in each one ask the same few questions: could someone fall, could something burn, could something poison or choke or strangle, could something fall or cut or crush, could water and electricity meet. Then fix what you find before you leave the room, because a danger is only handled once it is gone.

Chapter 22 · Improve Overall Safety. You have found and removed the hazards that were already in the home; now Safety is made to last. The next chapter completes the fourth S: the safeguards that keep new hazards from taking hold, the calm preparation for the emergencies you cannot prevent, and the habit that keeps the whole home safe long after today's hunt.

↑ Contents

Part Six · Safety

Chapter Twenty-Two

Improve Overall Safety

Finding and removing hazards makes a home safer today. But a home does not hold still, and some harm cannot be prevented at all, only prepared for. This chapter completes the fourth S by adding what removing cannot: the moves that keep new dangers from taking hold, and the protections that stand ready for the day something goes wrong anyway. See it, remove it, prevent it, prepare for it, and the home is safe.

You can now do two things you could not do when this part began. You can look at your home and see the hazards in it, the ones hiding in plain sight, because you have the lens. And you can remove them, thoroughly, room by room, because you have the hunt. Between them, those two skills have made your home meaningfully safer than it was, and if you stopped here you would have done real good.

But there is a reason this part has one more chapter, and it is a pair of honest facts about homes. The first is that a home does not hold still. The hunt you ran last chapter made the home safe as of that day, and then the day ended, and things began, quietly, to flow back. A new appliance arrives with a new cord. A child grows two inches and reaches a shelf that was safe last month. Batteries die. The hunt is a snapshot, and the home keeps moving after the shutter clicks. The second fact is harder and gentler: some harm cannot be removed in advance at all. You can clear every hazard you can find and a fire can still start, a person can still fall, and no amount of hunting will have prevented it. Those are not failures of your search. They are simply the part of safety that removing cannot reach.

So this chapter completes the fourth S by adding the two moves that a hazard hunt cannot make. The first is to keep new dangers from taking hold, so the home does not quietly undo the work you did. The second is to be ready for the harm you cannot prevent, so that on the worst day the home is on your side. See it, remove it, prevent it, prepare for it. With the last two, Safety is whole, and the home is not just cleared of today's dangers but genuinely, durably safe.

In this chapter

  • See why removing hazards, on its own, is not enough to keep a home safe.
  • Raise the home's baseline instead of chasing hazards one at a time.
  • Prevent new hazards by making the safe way the easy way.
  • Prepare for the harm you cannot prevent, with working alarms, an extinguisher, and a walked exit plan.
  • See the whole of Safety as four moves, and complete the fourth S.

The reframeFrom Removing to Improving

Everything so far in this part has been about subtraction: find a danger, take it out. That is the right place to start, and it is not the place to stop, because subtraction alone leaves you doing the same work forever.

Improving overall safety

Improving overall safety is the work beyond removing today's hazards: preventing new ones from taking hold, and preparing for the harm you cannot prevent. Removing hazards makes a home safe now. Prevention and preparation are what keep it safe.

You can chase hazards one at a time forever, or you can raise the whole home's floor so it is harder to get hurt in at all. Overall safety is the second thing: not a longer list of dangers removed, but a home that is safer even against the ones you have not met yet.

Think of the difference between bailing a boat and fixing the leak. Removing hazards is bailing: necessary, effective, and endless, because the water keeps coming. Improving overall safety is the other kind of work, the kind that changes the boat itself so less water gets in and so you are ready if it does. You will still bail now and then; the hunt is not retired. But once the home's baseline is higher, the bailing gets rarer and matters less, because you are no longer depending on catching every single hazard by hand, one at a time, forever. That is a good thing, because catching every hazard by hand, forever, is exactly the kind of vigilance the last chapter warned does not scale.

Raising the baseline has two halves, and the rest of this chapter is those two halves. One looks forward at the hazards that have not arrived yet and keeps them from taking hold. The other looks at the harm that no prevention can stop and gets the home ready to meet it. Prevention and preparation. Together they are what turns a home that has been made safe into a home that stays safe.

The first movePrevent: Keep New Hazards From Taking Hold

Start with the leaks. A hunted home drifts back toward hazard not because anyone is careless but because ordinary life brings new things in, and some of them are dangerous, and the dangerous ones do not announce themselves any more than the last batch did.

A hunt clears the hazards that are here. Prevention is what keeps the next one from quietly taking their place, because a home does not stay hunted. It drifts, and things flow back in, and the only defense that scales is making the safe way the easy way.

That last phrase is the whole of prevention, and it is worth taking seriously, because it is the opposite of willpower. You will not keep your home safe by resolving to be more careful, any more than you kept it tidy by resolving to be neater; you proved that to yourself back in Straighten. What works is design. You make the safe way the easy way, so that staying safe is what naturally happens when everyone just does the convenient thing.

Make the safe way the easy way, so hazards stop coming back: choose the safer default, give the dangerous things a home, and re-hunt now and then to catch what has drifted in.

In practice that is three small habits. The first is to choose the safer default when something new comes into the house, at the one moment it is easiest to do, which is the moment it arrives. The heater you buy is the one that switches itself off if it tips; the cleaner you replace runs out into a cupboard that already has a latch. You are not adding a chore; you are just steering the ordinary decision, once, toward safe. The second is to give the dangerous things a home, the same move you learned in Straighten, now aimed at safety: the medicines live in one latched box and go back into it every time, the knives live in the block, the button batteries live up high, so that "away" and "safe" are the same place and putting a thing away is what makes it safe. The third is to run the hunt again, lightly, now and then, not as a project but as a habit, a slow walk with the five questions every so often, so the drift is caught while it is small. Nothing here is a schedule to be written down and enforced; that kind of documented standard is a later S. This is just the safe way, made easy enough that it happens on its own.

The second movePrepare: Ready for What You Cannot Prevent

Now the harder, gentler half, the one that is not about hazards at all. However well you prevent, some harm will always sit outside your reach. A fire can start in a wall you cannot see. Carbon monoxide has no smell and gives no warning your body can catch. A person can fall on a night when nothing was wrong with the floor. You cannot remove these in advance, and pretending you can is not safety; it is just anxiety with extra steps. What you can do is prepare, so that on the day one of them comes, the home meets it ready.

Some harm you cannot prevent, only prepare for. You cannot promise a fire will never start. You can promise that the alarm will wake you and that the way out is clear. Preparation is love for the day you hope never comes.

Preparation, like prevention, is a short and concrete list, not a state of dread.

Put the protections in place for the harm you cannot prevent: working smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms you keep alive, a fire extinguisher within reach, an exit everyone has walked, and the few numbers and steps everyone knows.

The center of it is the alarm, because it is the one protection that has to work while you are unconscious. A working smoke alarm, and a carbon-monoxide alarm where there is anything that burns fuel, on every floor and near the bedrooms, is the single highest-value thing in this whole chapter, and its whole value depends on one unglamorous fact: it has to actually work, which means it has to be tested and its battery kept alive, or it is a plastic disc that does nothing. Beyond the alarm, the list is calm and finite. A fire extinguisher within reach of the kitchen, where most home fires begin, and a rough sense of how to use it. A way out of every room, ideally two, and an exit plan the household has actually walked, from the bedrooms to a single meeting spot outside, so that in the dark and the noise nobody has to invent a plan. And the few plain numbers and steps everyone should know, including the children, so that the knowledge does not live only in one head. That is the whole of it. Not a bunker. A prepared home.

Quick Win

Test every smoke and carbon-monoxide alarm in the home right now, one press each, and note any floor that has none. Working alarms are the highest-value protection in the house, and the only one that has to keep working while you are asleep.

6S Tip

Keep the tools of preparation in one known place, a single shelf or box: the spare alarm batteries, the fire extinguisher, a flashlight, the first-aid kit. Preparation you cannot find in the dark is not preparation.

All four movesThe Whole of Safety

Step back now and look at the fourth S whole, because you have just finished it, and it turns out to have been four moves all along, each the answer to a question the one before it could not ask.

You learned to see the hazard, by changing the question you asked the home from "is it tidy?" to "could this hurt someone?". You learned to remove it, thoroughly, room by room, fixing each danger the moment you found it. You have now learned to prevent the next one, by making the safe way the easy way so the home stops drifting back. And you have learned to prepare for the harm that none of that can stop, so the home is ready on its worst day. See it, remove it, prevent it, prepare for it. That is not a checklist to run once; it is a way of holding your home that, once you have it, you do not really put down.

And notice what it is not. It is not the exhausting vigilance the last chapter warned against, the impossible job of watching everything forever. Each of the four moves is the opposite of vigilance: it is a piece of work you do deliberately, once or now and then, precisely so that you can stop watching. The professionals give the goal a stark name, zero accidents and injuries, and it can sound cold, but read it as what it is, a direction rather than a destination you will ever tick off. You will not achieve a mathematically perfect home. You are simply always turned that way, and being turned that way, with these four moves in hand, is what safety consciousness actually is: not fear held at a high pitch, but a steady, low, permanent habit of care that mostly runs quietly in the background of an ordinary, happy home.

Family Challenge

Walk the exit plan together, calmly, once. From each bedroom, how do you get out, and where does everyone meet outside? Children who have walked it once remember it, and walking it turns a frightening idea into a known, ordinary thing.

The milestoneThe Needle Reaches Safety Complete

Go and look at the friction meter, because it has reached a mark, and it is a mark that has been a long time coming.

The needle has moved to the fourth milestone on the dial, the one labeled Safety complete, and it sits there now beside Sort complete, Straighten complete, and Shine complete. Four of the six S's are done. Look at how far the needle has traveled from where it started, back in the clutter, and let that land for a moment, because it is real: the home is cleared, arranged, kept clean on a rhythm, and now safe, its hazards gone, new ones kept from taking hold, and its worst days prepared for.

Finding hazards makes a home safer once. Preventing them and preparing for them keep it safe for good.

The step onto this mark was small, and that is honest, and it does not diminish the milestone. It was small because the big daily friction was cleared long ago, in Sort and Straighten and Shine, and what these three safety chapters added was a different kind of gain, the removal not of everyday friction but of the friction of the worst day, the harm kept from happening and the emergency the home is now ready to meet. That gain is quiet on a dial that mostly measures the texture of ordinary days, and it is one of the most valuable things in the whole book. The mark is a true arrival, the fourth S finished. And the goal, out on the calm side, is still ahead, because the needle reaches it only at the very end, when everything you have built is not just built but made to last. Two S's remain to do that. The home is safe. The next work is to keep it, all of it, this way.

In closingSafety, Complete

That is Part Six, and it is the fourth S, done. It is worth marking, because it was a turn in the book: for the first nineteen chapters you worked on the state of the room, and in these three you turned to the people in it, which was always the more important thing.

You did it in three moves that added up to four. In Chapter 20 you learned to see, trading the question "is it tidy?" for "could this hurt someone?", and you did a first pass on the obvious dangers. In Chapter 21 you learned to remove, carrying the five questions through the whole home and fixing each hazard the moment you found it. And in this chapter you learned to keep the home safe, preventing new hazards from taking hold and preparing for the harm you cannot prevent. A home that is cleared, arranged, clean, and now safe is a genuinely good home to live in, and you have built one.

What is left is not more building; it is holding. Everything you have made across these twenty-two chapters lives, for now, largely in your head and your hands: it works because you know how it works and you keep it going. The last two S's are about changing that, so the home holds its shape without leaning on any one person, and keeps holding it over years. That work begins in the next chapter. For now, the fourth S is complete, and your home is safe. Take the win.

Common Mistake

Fitting a smoke alarm, feeling safe, and never testing it again, so the one protection you were counting on is silent the night it matters. A protection you do not keep alive is only decoration. Give the button a press whenever the clocks change.

One Idea to Keep

Safety is four moves, and you now have them all: see the hazard, remove it, prevent the next one, and prepare for the harm you cannot stop. A safe home is not one where nothing can ever go wrong. It is one that is ready when it does.

Chapter 23 · Standardize: The Best Way We Know Today. Your home is now sorted, arranged, clean, and safe, and all of that lives largely in your head and your hands. The next chapter opens Part Seven and the fifth S, Standardize, which is how you write down the best way you have found so it holds steady, does not drift back, and no longer depends on you alone.

↑ Contents

Part Seven · Standardize

Chapter Twenty-Three

Standardize: The Best Way We Know Today

Everything you have built so far lives in your head and your hands, which means it lasts exactly as long as your memory and your energy do. Standardize is how the best way stops depending on you: you write it down. A standard is not a rule carved in stone, it is the best way you know today, held in place only until you find a better one.

Stand back and look at what you have built. A home cleared of what does not belong, arranged so everything has a place, kept clean on a light rhythm, and made safe for the people in it. Four of the six S's, done. It is a genuinely good home, and you should feel good about it.

Now notice something a little uncomfortable about it. Almost all of it lives in exactly one place, and that place is you. You know which drawer things go back into, and why. You know the best way to load the dishwasher so everything actually gets clean, and the order of the bedtime routine that makes it go smoothly, and the trick with the launch pad that keeps the mornings calm. Nobody wrote any of it down, because you did not need to; you simply know it. Which means the home you built works beautifully, right up until the day you are sick, or away, or just tired and out of patience, and then it quietly stops working, because the person it was all running on is not available, and the good ways were never anywhere but in your head.

That is the gap the fifth S closes, and it is why Standardize exists. Standardize is not about adding rules or turning your warm home into an office with procedures. It is about taking the good ways you have already found, the ones that currently live in your memory and your hands, and writing them down, so they stop depending on you. That is the whole of it, and it is more of a relief than it sounds, because it means you finally get to set down a weight you have been carrying without noticing: the weight of being the only person who knows how the home works.

In this chapter

  • See why the good ways you have built drift back when they live only in your head.
  • Understand what a standard actually is: the best way you know today, written down.
  • Treat a standard as a recipe, not a rule, so it stays human and easy to follow.
  • Keep a standard living by rewriting it the moment someone finds a better way.
  • Write your first standard for a recurring task and put it where the work happens.

The problemWhy Things Drift Back

You have probably noticed, over the course of this book, a quiet worry running underneath the work: will it last? You sort a drawer and it is perfect, and some part of you knows that in three months it could be a mess again. That worry is not paranoia. It is an accurate reading of how homes behave, and it is exactly what this S is built to answer.

Everything you have built so far lives in your head and your hands, which means it lasts exactly as long as your memory and your energy do. A standard is how a good way of doing something stops depending on you.

Things drift back for a reason that has nothing to do with anyone being lazy or careless. They drift back because a way of doing something that lives only in one person's head is invisible to everyone else, so everyone else does it their own way, and "their own way" is rarely the way you worked out. You put the mixing bowls in the low cupboard for a good reason; someone who does not know the reason puts them back on the counter, and now the system you designed is quietly being undone by a person who is genuinely trying to help. Multiply that by every task in the home and every person in it, and the drift is not a moral failing. It is just what happens when the best way is a secret.

The people who first named these steps, on the factory floors of Toyota, saw the same thing and gave this S a blunt job: prevent reversion back to the old way. Not through willpower or nagging, but by making the good way visible and shared, so that following it is the easy, obvious thing and everyone is working from the same page. A standard is how you make the best way visible. It is the difference between a home that holds its shape and one that slowly slides back the moment your attention moves elsewhere.

The reframeA Standard Is a Recipe

So let me say plainly what a standard is, because the word itself does the chapter a disservice. "Standard" sounds cold. It sounds like rules, clipboards, and someone checking whether you complied. Put all of that out of your mind, because a home standard is a much warmer and simpler thing.

A standard is not bureaucracy. It is a recipe: the best way you know to make something turn out right, written down so it turns out right every time, for anyone, even on a tired day.

Think about an actual recipe, the kind on a card in a kitchen. It is not a rule anyone is enforcing. It is a gift: someone worked out how to make the thing turn out well, and they wrote it down, so that you do not have to work it out again from scratch, and so it comes out right whether you are sharp that day or half asleep. A recipe takes skill that lived in one person's hands and makes it available to anyone who can read. That is precisely what a home standard does, for the recurring tasks of a home instead of for a cake.

What a standard is

A standard is the current best way to do a recurring task, written down plainly enough that anyone in the home can follow it and get the same result, and kept open enough that it is rewritten the moment a better way is found.

Notice what that definition asks for and what it does not. It asks that the way be the best you currently know, written plainly, and followable by anyone. It does not ask for length, formality, or completeness. A good home standard is usually a few lines, in plain words, about one task. If it is so long or so fussy that nobody will read it, it has failed on the one thing that matters, which is being used. The test of a standard is never how thorough it looks. It is whether the next person actually follows it and gets the result you would have gotten.

The living standardThe Best Way We Know Today

There is one more word in the title, and it is the most important one, because it is what keeps a standard from becoming the very cage people fear.

The word in the title doing the quiet work is today. A standard is not the last word, it is the current best word, and the moment someone finds a better way, the standard is not broken. It is simply what you improve.

This matters more than it might seem, because it dissolves the main objection to standardizing anything at home, which is a good and healthy objection: I do not want to lock the household into one rigid way of doing things forever. You are right not to want that, and a standard, properly understood, is the opposite of that. A standard is a starting point, not a finish line. It captures the best way you know as of today, so that you are not forever reinventing it, and it stays fully open to being replaced the moment someone works out something better. When your teenager finds a faster way to fold the laundry, the standard does not win the argument by virtue of being written down. The better way wins, and then you spend thirty seconds updating the card, and now the better way is the standard.

Held that way, a standard is not a constraint on improvement; it is the thing that makes improvement stick. Without a written standard, a good new idea gets used once and forgotten. With one, the improvement gets captured, and the next person starts from there instead of from scratch. The card on the cupboard door is not the household's rule-book. It is its running record of the best way anyone has found so far, and the whole point of writing it in pencil, so to speak, is that it is meant to be improved.

A standard is not a rule carved in stone. It is the best way you have found so far, held in place only until you find a better one, and then rewritten without ceremony.

The worked exampleWrite Your First Standard

Enough concept. Let me walk you through making one, because it is much smaller than it sounds, and doing one is the fastest way to feel how light a standard really is. Pick a single recurring task that mostly works only when you do it. Not the hardest thing in the home; the opposite. Choose something small and ordinary that you have quietly become the keeper of, loading the dishwasher, the morning launch-pad routine, taking out the recycling on the right night in the right way. Now, instead of inventing a "best way", just capture the one you already use, because you have almost certainly worked out a good way already without ever writing it down. Watch yourself do the task once, and write the steps as you go, in plain words, as few as will do the job. Most home tasks come down to three to six steps. If you find yourself writing step eleven, you are describing your personal quirks, not the task; cut back to the handful of steps that actually matter to the result.

Then, and this is the part people skip, put the standard where the task happens, not in a folder somewhere sensible. A dishwasher standard lives taped inside the cabinet above the dishwasher, not in a binder in the office. The whole value of a standard is that the next person meets it at the moment they need it, and a perfect document nobody opens is worth less than three scrappy lines stuck in the right spot. And there is a lovely shortcut for finding the best way in the first place: if someone in the home already does a task better than everyone else, do not invent a standard from scratch, just ask them to show you, and write down what they do. The best way usually already exists, fully formed, in somebody's hands. A standard is often just the act of making one person's good habit into everyone's.

Quick Win

Pick one recurring thing that only really works when you do it, loading the dishwasher, the bedtime routine, taking out the recycling, and write down the best way in five plain steps. Stick it where the task happens. One standard, today.

6S Tip

Write the standard where the work happens, not in a binder. A note taped inside the cupboard door beats a perfect document nobody opens. The best standard is the one you cannot avoid seeing.

The milestoneThe Needle Holds, and Stops Sliding Back

Go and look at the friction meter, and this time notice what it does not do. It does not move. And that is not a disappointment; it is the whole point of this S, showing up honestly on the dial.

Every chapter until now, the needle traveled because the home changed: clutter left, things found homes, surfaces got clean and read, dangers were removed. This chapter changed nothing in the rooms. You wrote down a way of doing something you were already doing. Nothing was cleared, so the needle holds exactly where Safety left it, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

A standard is the best way you know today, written down.

But look closer, because for the first time the dial shows something new, and it is behind the needle rather than ahead of it. Until now, every gain the needle recorded was quietly reversible. A sorted room can re-clutter. A clean surface re-soils. A good habit lapses. Every position the needle ever reached, it could also slide back from, and some part of you has known that all along. Standardize is the first S whose job is not to move the needle forward but to keep it from sliding back, so a small catch appears behind the needle, a ratchet holding it against the pull toward friction, and the backslide that used to be always possible is, for the first time, blocked. The needle did not advance today. It got something arguably more valuable: it stopped being able to retreat. The goal is still ahead on the calm side, because Standardize has only begun and Sustain still follows, and holding a gain in place is exactly the work these last two S's exist to do.

Family Challenge

Ask the person who does a task best to teach it to everyone else, and write down what they do. The best way usually already lives in someone's hands; a standard just makes it everyone's.

In closingStandardize Has Only Begun

You changed nothing in the rooms this chapter, and you may have changed something more durable than any single room: you took one good way of doing things out of your own head and put it where the whole household can reach it. That is the fifth S in its smallest form, and it is the move that makes everything before it capable of lasting.

What you have not done yet is the rest of it, and that is deliberate. One card on one cupboard door is a proof of concept, not a system. Turning a handful of standards into something the whole home runs on takes a few more tools: a way to make sure recurring work actually happens and nothing is forgotten, a sense of when things get done and by whom, and, for the tasks where a picture beats a paragraph, a way to show the right result rather than describe it. Those are the next two chapters. For now, hold on to the one idea that all of Standardize grows from, which is also the warmest way to think about it: you are not writing rules, you are writing down the best way you know today, so that the good you have built can be followed by anyone and improved by everyone.

Common Mistake

Writing a standard as a strict rule and then defending it forever. A standard you are not allowed to change becomes a cage, and people quietly route around a cage. Keep it the best way for now, and let anyone propose a better one.

One Idea to Keep

Write down the best way you know today. It takes the good you have built out of your head and your hands and puts it somewhere it can hold without you, be followed by anyone, and be improved by everyone. That is all a standard is, and it is how the gains last.
