The next chapter turns standards into the things that carry them: checklists so nothing is forgotten, schedules so recurring work has a time, and responsibilities so every standard has a name attached to it.

↑ Contents

Part Seven · Standardize

Chapter Twenty-Four

Checklists, Schedules, and Responsibilities

A standard is a recipe on a card, and a recipe on a card does not cook itself. A standard actually runs when three things are true: someone knows exactly what to do, the work has a time, and someone owns it. This chapter gives every standard its three tools: a checklist for the what, a schedule for the when, and a name for the who.

Last chapter you wrote a standard: you took the best way you knew to do some recurring task and put it on a card where anyone could follow it. That was the crucial first move, and it is not, by itself, enough, as you may already have discovered if you wrote one and then watched it get ignored for a week.

The problem is simple and worth saying plainly. A standard is a recipe on a card, and a recipe on a card does not cook itself. Writing down the best way tells everyone what good looks like, but knowing what good looks like has never once been the same as doing it. The card can be perfect and still sit there, because a standard, to actually run, needs three things to be true that writing it down does not supply. Someone has to know exactly what to do, step by step, without holding it in their head. The work has to have a time, or it waits forever for a moment that never feels right. And someone has to own it, or everyone assumes someone else will.

Those three needs are the whole of this chapter, and each has a tool that answers it. A checklist answers what. A schedule answers when. A responsibility answers who. Give a standard all three and it stops being a hopeful card on the fridge and becomes a small piece of machinery that runs whether or not you are thinking about it. That is the difference between a home that has good intentions written down and a home that actually keeps its shape.

In this chapter

  • See why a written standard, on its own, still does not get followed.
  • Turn a standard into a checklist, so nothing gets forgotten.
  • Give recurring work a schedule, so it happens on a rhythm instead of in a crisis.
  • Put a name on every standard, so someone owns it.
  • Combine the three tools into a simple home system that runs without you.

The gapWhy a Standard on a Card Is Not Enough

It helps to be precise about how a good standard fails, because each way it fails points straight at the tool that fixes it. Watch a written standard that nobody follows, and you will see it fall down in one of exactly three places.

The first is memory. The standard has six steps and the person doing it remembers four, not because they are careless but because that is what human memory does under a normal amount of distraction, so two steps quietly get dropped every time. The second is timing. Everyone agrees the task matters and everyone means to do it, but it has no particular moment attached, so it drifts to "later", and "later" is where good intentions go to die. The third is ownership. The task belongs to the household in general, which means it belongs to no one in particular, so each person assumes another has it, and it sits undone in the exact center of everyone's blind spot.

Notice that none of these three failures is a failure of the standard itself. The card was fine. What was missing was a way to carry it: something to hold the steps so none are forgotten, something to attach it to a time so it happens, and something to pin it to a person so it is owned. Those three carriers are the checklist, the schedule, and the responsibility, and the rest of this chapter is simply one each.

To make a standard run without you

To make a standard run without you, answer three questions. What: a checklist, so nothing is forgotten. When: a schedule, so the work has a time and happens on a rhythm. Who: a responsibility, so one name owns it. A standard with all three stops being a good idea on a card and becomes something the home does on its own.

The whatThe Checklist: So Nothing Is Forgotten

Start with memory, because it is the one people are most embarrassed by and least need to be. A checklist takes a standard and turns it into a list you run rather than a thing you recall, and the moment you have one, forgetting a step stops being possible in the ordinary way.

A checklist is not a sign that you are forgetful. It is what lets a capable person do a complicated thing perfectly without holding all of it in their head. Pilots and surgeons live by them, and not because they are bad at their jobs, but because everyone forgets, and a list does not.

That is worth dwelling on, because a lot of people resist checklists at home out of a quiet sense that needing one is admitting a weakness. It is the opposite. The people who fly planes and operate on hearts, who are about as capable and well-trained as humans get, do not trust their memory for the steps that matter, and their results got dramatically better the day they stopped. A checklist is not a crutch for the incompetent; it is how the competent stay reliable when they are tired, rushed, or interrupted, which at home is roughly always. The trick is only to keep it short and real: the few steps that actually change the result, in plain words, not every conceivable detail. A checklist you will actually run beats a thorough one you will not, every time.

The whenThe Schedule: So It Actually Happens

Now timing, which is where more good standards die than anywhere else. A standard can be perfectly clear and perfectly owned and still never happen, simply because it never has a particular time, and a task with no time does not sit patiently waiting to be convenient. It waits to become urgent.

A task with no time does not get done on a rhythm. It gets done in a panic, once it has become a crisis. A schedule is how you trade the occasional emergency for the small, dull, ordinary upkeep that quietly prevents it.

This is the whole quiet economy of a schedule. The gutter you never clean on a rhythm is the gutter you eventually clean in the rain because it overflowed; the fridge nobody wipes on a schedule is the one you empty in a hurry when something has gone off. Upkeep is boring precisely because it is working, and the way you get boring, working upkeep instead of dramatic, expensive crises is to give recurring work a time before it demands one. The easiest way to do that is not to invent a new slot in an already full week but to hang the task off something that already happens: the bins go out the night the show you watch ends, the plants get watered when the Sunday coffee is brewing. Attached to an existing rhythm, a task stops depending on anyone remembering to schedule it, because the schedule is already running.

The whoThe Responsibility: So Someone Owns It

Last, ownership, which is the one most likely to cause a flicker of discomfort, because it sounds like assigning chores and standing over people. Held rightly, it is nothing of the sort. It is just making sure each standard has a name attached, so it is somebody's, because a task that is everybody's is, reliably and always, nobody's.

A job that belongs to everyone belongs to no one. You met that line back in Shine, and it is even truer of a standard: the fastest way to make sure something never happens is to leave it unowned, so that every person assumes some other person has it handled.

You met that principle when you divided up the cleaning, and it applies without change here: a standard with no name against it is a standard in freefall, because responsibility that is diffuse is responsibility that evaporates. The fix is a name, one name, per standard. But how you attach the name matters as much as that you do, and this is where a home is not a workplace. You do not hand out the jobs; wherever you can, you let people choose them, because a job someone chose is a job they will actually do, and a job that was dropped on them is a job they will quietly resent and half-perform. Sit the household down, lay out the standards that need owners, and let people pick. The one who does not mind the bins takes the bins. What is chosen gets done; what is imposed gets subverted, slowly, and usually with excellent excuses.

The worked examplePut the Three Together

None of this is heavy, and the fastest way to feel that is to take a single standard and give it all three tools at once, which takes about five minutes and changes the standard entirely.

Take the after-dinner reset, the light fifteen-minute pass you met back in Shine. As a standard, it is the best way you know to get the common rooms back to calm before bed. Now give it the tools. The checklist is four or five lines: clear the table, wipe the counters, start the dishwasher, ten minutes of everyone putting their own things away, lights and lock. The schedule is not a new appointment; it is a cue you already have, so the reset starts when the dinner plates are cleared, every night, no decision required. And the responsibilities are chosen, not handed down: one person has the kitchen, another has the living room, the kids each have their own things, and the youngest, who asked, gets the very important job of the light switches. Written on one small card and stuck to the side of the fridge, that is no longer a vague good intention. It is a fifteen-minute machine with a list, a time, and named parts, and it will run on a tired Tuesday when nobody can be bothered, which is the only real test any of this has to pass.

Quick Win

Take the one standard you wrote last chapter and give it the three tools in five minutes: turn it into a short checklist, hang it off a time or an existing cue, and put one name against it. That is the difference between a standard that exists and a standard that happens.

6S Tip

Hang the checklist and the schedule where the work happens and where everyone passes, the fridge, the back of a door, and keep both short. A checklist nobody can find, or one so long nobody finishes it, is the same as no checklist at all.

The milestoneThe Needle Holds, and the Catch Gets Stronger

Go and look at the friction meter, and you will find it exactly where it was last chapter. It has not moved, and, as before, that is honest rather than disappointing. You did not clear any new friction this chapter; you built tools for the standards you already had. Nothing left the rooms, so the needle holds.

A standard is the best way. A checklist, a schedule, and a name are what make the best way actually happen.

But look again at the small catch that appeared behind the needle last chapter, the one that keeps a gain from sliding back, because it is sturdier now. A written standard was the first thing that could hold a gain in place at all; a standard with a checklist, a schedule, and a name is a much stronger hold, because now the good way is not just recorded but carried, run on a rhythm, and owned by someone. Where last chapter's catch was a single tooth, this chapter has given it three, and the backslide it prevents is barred more firmly than before. The needle did not advance. The grip on everything behind it got noticeably tighter, and that is precisely the work of this S. The goal is still ahead on the calm side, because one piece of Standardize remains and Sustain still follows.

Family Challenge

Build one checklist together for a shared recurring job, the after-dinner reset, the Saturday tidy, and let each person choose the line they will own. A job you chose gets done; a job you were handed gets resented.

In closingStandardize, Nearly Whole

You have most of the fifth S now. Chapter 23 gave you the idea of a standard, the best way you know today, written down. This chapter gave you the three tools that turn a written standard into something that runs: a checklist so nothing is forgotten, a schedule so it happens, and a name so it is owned. Between them, a concept and its tools, you can take almost any recurring task in the home and make it hold its shape without leaning on your memory or your patience.

There is one kind of standard left, and it is the kind where all the words in the world work less well than a single picture. Some things are far easier to show than to describe: what a "tidy" shelf actually looks like, how the cables should be coiled, where exactly each thing sits when the room is right. For those, the best standard is not a checklist but an image, and building that last kind, the visual standard, is the next chapter, and it completes Standardize. For now, you have turned good intentions into small machines, and that is most of the way to a home that keeps itself.

Common Mistake

Making the checklist so complete it becomes a chore in itself, or the schedule so ambitious nobody keeps it. The three tools are meant to make a standard lighter, not heavier. If a tool is adding work instead of removing worry, cut it back until it helps.

One Idea to Keep

A written standard is a good idea; a checklist, a schedule, and a name are what make it happen. Give every standard you care about a list so nothing is forgotten, a time so it gets done on a rhythm, and a name so someone owns it, and it will run without you.

The next chapter builds the standards a picture carries better than any list, a photo of the ideal state, a simple storyboard, the visual that shows the right result at a glance, and completes the fifth S.

↑ Contents

Part Seven · Standardize

Chapter Twenty-Five

Pictures, Storyboards, and Visual Standards

Some things are far easier to show than to say. A written standard tells you what to do; a visual standard shows you what right looks like. This chapter adds the last kind of standard, the one a picture carries better than any list: a photo of the ideal state, and a short storyboard of the steps. With it, the fifth S is complete.

You have come a long way into the fifth S. You have the idea of a standard, the best way you know, written down where anyone can follow it. You have the three tools that make a standard actually run: a checklist so nothing is forgotten, a schedule so it has a time, and a name so someone owns it. For most of the recurring work of a home, that is enough, and it is a great deal.

But you have almost certainly run into the edge of it by now, the place where words start to strain. Try to write down, in sentences, exactly what a tidy shelf looks like, and you will find yourself piling up clauses that still do not quite capture it: mugs here, but not like that, spaced but not too spaced, and the whole thing somehow still comes out looking fussier and less clear than the shelf itself. Some things simply resist description. How the cables should be coiled and where they tuck. What the entryway looks like when it is genuinely reset. Where each thing sits when the room is right. For all of these, a paragraph is the wrong tool, and there is a far better one sitting in your pocket.

This chapter is that better tool: the visual standard, the standard you show instead of tell. It is the last kind of standard the fifth S needs, and adding it completes Standardize. When you have it, the parts of your home that were hardest to put into words become the easiest of all to keep, because "right" stops being a description someone has to interpret and becomes a picture they can simply match.

In this chapter

  • See where written standards run out, and why some things are far easier to show than to say.
  • Make an ideal-state photo: capture a space at its best so the photo becomes the standard.
  • Build a simple storyboard: show a task's steps as a short strip of pictures.
  • Shoot a visual standard so it is genuinely easy to match, and put it where the work happens.
  • Complete the fifth S, so your home runs on what you have made visible.

The mediumWhen Words Are Not Enough

There is a particular kind of standard that fails not because it is wrong but because it is written. Everyone reads the same careful sentences and pictures something slightly different, and slightly different, multiplied across a household, is exactly how a shelf that was meant to be uniform ends up looking like four people's separate guesses. The problem is not the people and not the standard. It is the medium.

A written standard tells you what to do. A visual standard shows you what right looks like. For anything you would struggle to put into words, that is the difference between a standard people argue about and one they can simply see and match.

A visual standard

A visual standard is the ideal state of a space or a task, captured as a picture rather than described in words: a photo of what "done" looks like, or a short storyboard of the steps. Where a written standard tells you what to do, a visual standard shows you what right looks like.

This is why "tidy" causes so many household arguments: it is a word, and words about how things should look are almost infinitely arguable. My tidy and your tidy are genuinely different pictures, and no amount of careful writing fully closes the gap, because we are trying to transmit an image through the narrow pipe of language and each person rebuilds it a little differently at the other end. The moment you stop describing the image and simply show it, the argument evaporates. There is nothing left to interpret. You are not comparing your idea of tidy to mine; we are both looking at the same photograph and comparing the shelf to it. The disagreement was never really about tidiness. It was about the fact that we were each holding a different picture, and a shared picture is the thing that fixes it.

The flagshipThe Picture of the Ideal State

So here is the flagship tool of this chapter, and it is almost comically simple, which is part of why it works.

Photograph a space when it is exactly right, and that photo becomes the standard: not a description of the ideal state, but a picture of it, that anyone can match their reality against at a glance.

That is the whole move. You get a space exactly the way it should be, the pantry, the coat closet, the play shelf, the desk, on one of those rare days when it is genuinely right, and before it drifts, you take a photograph. Then you put that photograph where the space is, taped inside the cupboard door or stuck to the wall beside the shelf, and from that moment the standard for that space is not in anyone's head or in any document. It is on the door.

The most powerful standard in a home is often a single photograph: the shelf, the counter, the entryway, captured on the day it was exactly right. From then on, tidy is not an opinion and not an argument. It is a picture on the cupboard door, and the room either matches it or it does not.

You have actually done a version of this before, at the very start, when you took a before photo of a space you were about to fix. That before photo was the visual baseline, the honest record of the mess. The ideal-state photo is its optimistic mirror image: not "this is what it looked like at its worst" but "this is what it looks like at its best, and this is what we are keeping it like." The same simple act of pointing a camera, aimed now at the target instead of the starting line. A child too young to read the word "tidy" can match a shelf to a photo, which is a fair sign of how low this tool sets the bar for being useful.

The sequenceThe Storyboard

A photo of the ideal state is perfect for a space that should look a certain way. But some standards are not about how a thing looks at rest; they are about a sequence, the steps of a task done in the right order, and for those, one photo is not enough. The answer is not to fall back on a paragraph. It is to use a few pictures instead of one.

For a task with steps, a short strip of pictures beats a paragraph. Show the few frames that matter, in order, and the next person can follow the pictures without reading a word.

This is a storyboard, borrowed, without any ceremony, from the way films are planned: a short strip of simple frames, each showing one key step, laid out in order. How the folding table gets set up and stowed. How the cables coil and where they clip. How the recycling gets sorted on collection night. For a task like these, three or four little pictures carry more, and carry it faster, than a whole numbered list, because the reader is not converting words into actions in their head; they are just copying what they see, frame by frame. You do not need to be a photographer or an artist. Four phone snaps of your own hands doing the steps, or four quick stick-figure sketches, are plenty. The value is entirely in the sequence being visible, not in the pictures being beautiful.

The craftMake It Match-able

A visual standard only works if it is genuinely easy to match, and there is a little craft to that, which is worth a paragraph because getting it slightly wrong is how good visual standards quietly stop being used.

Shoot the picture from the angle and in the light that the person will actually have when they go to set the space right. A photo of the pantry taken from a stepladder, when everyone else sees the pantry from standing height, is subtly hard to match, and subtly hard to match means quietly abandoned. Get down or up to the real eye line, use the ordinary light of the room, and capture the space the way it is actually seen. Then put the standard where the work happens, not in a folder somewhere sensible; a visual standard filed away is a contradiction in terms, because its entire value is being seen at the point of use. And keep it honest rather than impressive. A few slightly imperfect photos taped where they are needed will do more for your home than a beautiful laminated binder of visual standards that lives in a drawer and helps no one.

Quick Win

Photograph one space when it is exactly the way you want it, print it small, and tape it up where the space is. Now "put it back the way it should be" is not an instruction anyone has to remember or interpret. It is a picture to match.

6S Tip

Shoot the standard photo from the exact angle and in the same light someone will see the space from when they go to set it right. A picture shot from an odd angle or in different light is hard to match, and a standard that is hard to match is one people quietly stop using.

The milestoneThe Needle Reaches Standardize Complete

Go and look at the friction meter, because it has reached a mark, the fifth one on the dial.

Some things are easier to show than to say. When a picture carries the standard better than words can, the picture is the standard.

The needle sits now at the Standardize-complete tick, beside Sort complete, Straighten complete, Shine complete, and Safety complete. Five of the six S's are done. Notice that the tick forward was small, and that is honest: Standardize was never about clearing big new friction, the way Sort and Straighten and Shine were. Its whole gift was different, and quieter, and you can see it in the one part of the dial that has genuinely changed across this part. Look behind the needle, at the small catch that first appeared when you began to standardize and grew stronger when you gave standards their tools. It is fully engaged now, locked. Everything you have built across twenty-five chapters is written down, carried by checklists and schedules and names, and, where words fell short, shown in pictures, which means for the first time it is held against the slide back about as firmly as a home can be. The needle barely moved, and the grip behind it is complete. That is exactly what finishing this S was supposed to feel like. The goal is a step away on the calm side, because one S still remains, Sustain, which is the work of keeping a held home held not just today but over all the years to come.

Family Challenge

Let the children take the ideal-state photos and put them up at their own height. A child who took the picture of the tidy shelf is far more likely to put that shelf back the way the picture shows, because the standard is theirs.

In closingStandardize, Complete

That is Part Seven, and it is the fifth S, done. It is worth pausing on, because it changed the nature of what you have built. For the first six parts of this book you made your home good: cleared, arranged, clean, and safe. Standardize did something different. It made that goodness durable, took it out of your head and your hands and your good days, and put it somewhere it can survive a tired week and a house full of other people.

You did it in three moves. In Chapter 23 you learned what a standard is and wrote the first one down: the best way you know today, captured on a card. In Chapter 24 you gave standards the three tools that make them run: a checklist for the what, a schedule for the when, a name for the who. And in this chapter you added the last kind, the standard a picture carries better than any words: the ideal-state photo, the storyboard, the visual standard.

With this, the fifth S is complete. The best way you know is written down, carried by a checklist and a schedule and a name, and, where words fall short, shown in a picture. Your home no longer runs on your memory. It runs on what you have made visible.

There is one S left, and it is the one that turns all of this from an achievement into a way of life. You have built a home that is good and, now, held. What you have not yet done is keep it, not for a proud month but for years, through moves and new babies and busy seasons and every ordinary force that pulls a home back toward chaos. That work, the sixth S, is Sustain, and it is the whole of the last part. For now, stand back and look at what a standardized home actually is: not a home that depends on you remembering, but one that shows everyone, plainly, what right looks like.

Common Mistake

Building an elaborate laminated binder of visual standards that looks impressive and helps no one, instead of a few honest photos stuck where the work happens. The whole value of a visual standard is being seen at the point of use; a beautiful one filed away is worth nothing.

One Idea to Keep

When words fall short, show the result instead. Photograph a space at its best, or storyboard a task's steps, and put the picture where the work happens. Right stops being an argument and becomes something anyone can see and match.

Chapter 26 · Sustain: Keeping the Gains. Your home is now sorted, arranged, clean, safe, and standardized, built and, for the first time, fully held against sliding back. The next chapter opens Part Eight and the sixth and final S, Sustain, the work of keeping all of it, not for a week or a season but over the years, so the whole thing holds for good.

Part Eight · Sustain

Chapter Twenty-Six

Sustain: Keeping the Gains

You have built a home that is sorted, arranged, clean, safe, and standardized, and, with the fifth S, held against sliding back. But held is not the same as kept, because the world is relentless and nothing stays good on its own. Sustain is the sixth S and the only one you never finish: not a step you complete, but the quiet, ongoing habit of keeping the other five alive, for years, until keeping the home becomes simply how you live.

Look at what you have made. A home cleared of what does not belong, arranged so everything has a place, kept clean on a light rhythm, made safe for the people in it, and now, with Standardize, written down and shown in pictures so it holds its shape without leaning on your memory. Five of the six S's are done, and the fifth one locked the gains in place so they cannot quietly slide back through forgetting. It is a real achievement, and you should feel the weight of it.

And here is the last thing this book has to tell you, the thing the sixth S exists for. Held is not the same as kept. Standardize stopped your home from drifting back on its own, from the slow entropy of people forgetting the best way, and that is a great deal. But it cannot stop the world, and the world is relentless. Life keeps arriving: new things come through the door, the seasons turn over the contents of the house, children grow and their needs change, people move in and out, and every so often a busy or sad or chaotic season rolls through and no standard, however good, survives it untended. A home is not a machine you can set and leave running. It is a living thing, and living things have to be kept alive.

That keeping is the sixth S, Sustain, and it is different in kind from the five before it. Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, and Standardize are all things you do and, eventually, finish. Sustain is the one you never finish, because it is not a task with an end at all. It is the ongoing habit of keeping the other five alive, for as long as you live in the home, and the whole of this last part of the book is about how to make that keeping small enough, and shared enough, and natural enough that it lasts not for a proud month but for years.

In this chapter

  • See why a home that is held against sliding back still needs keeping over time.
  • Escape the "done" trap: understand that 6S is kept, not finished.
  • Build keeping on habit rather than willpower, so it survives your worst weeks.
  • Frame keeping as lighter than fixing, and as a shared choice rather than one person's burden.
  • Aim at second nature: the point where keeping the home is simply how you live.

The distinctionHeld Is Not Kept

It is worth being precise about the difference between what Standardize did and what Sustain has to do, because they are easy to blur and the gap between them is exactly where homes fall apart.

Nothing you have built will stay built on its own, and not because your standards are weak. It is because life is relentless: new things arrive, seasons change, people come and go, and the pull back toward chaos never takes a single day off. Sustain is not distrust of your standards. It is respect for how hard the world pushes on them.

Standardize dealt with the passive slide, the way a system quietly decays when people forget the best way or drift into doing it differently. A written, tool-carried, visible standard fixes that: it holds the shape. But there is a second force on your home that no standard can hold back, and it is not passive at all. It is the active, ceaseless arrival of life. A standard for the coat closet cannot stop three new coats from being bought; a beautiful pantry photo cannot stop a new baby from turning the whole household upside down for a year. These are not failures of your standards. They are just what living does, and it does it every single day, which is why the one thing you must never do is decide you are finished.

That is the trap the whole sixth S is built to help you avoid: the quiet, fatal moment when you look at your good home and think, "there, done." Because nothing in a home is ever done. The moment you believe it is, you stop tending it, and the relentless world, which never stopped for a second, begins carrying it back the way it came. A home is not a project you complete. It is a thing you keep.

The hero ideaYou Keep It, You Do Not Finish It

So let me state the central idea of this part as plainly as I can, because everything else in Sustain grows out of it.

You do not finish 6S. You keep it. The first five S's build a home worth keeping; the sixth is the habit of keeping it.

This is a genuine change in what you are doing, and it helps to name it. For twenty-five chapters you have been doing projects: bounded pieces of work with a beginning, a middle, and a satisfying end. Sort the drawer, and the drawer is sorted. Write the standard, and the standard is written. Sustain is not like that, and trying to treat it like that is why so many people's hard-won order collapses a few months after the big push.

The first five S's are things you do. Sustain is the one you keep doing, because it is not a step with an end but the ongoing life of the home.

Read that not as a burden but as a relief, because it quietly rewrites the job. You are no longer trying to reach some final, finished, perfect state and then defend it forever, which is exhausting and impossible. You are just living in your home and keeping it as you go, which is ordinary and human and light. Here, then, is the plain definition of the sixth S, and notice that it describes a way of being rather than a piece of work.

The sixth S

Sustain is the sixth S: the ongoing habit of keeping the first five alive, so the home stays sorted, arranged, clean, safe, and standardized not for a week or a season but over the years. It is the one S you never finish, because it is not a task you complete. It is a way of living.

The fuelHabit, Not Willpower

The obvious question is how, and the obvious wrong answer is "by trying harder", so let me close that door before you walk through it. You already know, from painful experience, that resolving to do better does not keep a home.

You will not keep your home by resolving to try harder, any more than you kept it tidy by resolving to be neater. Sustain runs on habit, not willpower: small, normal, shared, and low enough in effort that it survives the weeks when nobody has any energy to spare.

Willpower is the wrong fuel because it is exactly the thing that runs out first, and it runs out precisely when you need it most, in the busy, tired, difficult stretches that are also when a home most wants to fall apart. A keeping-plan that depends on everyone being motivated is a plan that works only on the days you least need it. Habit is different. A habit is something you do without deciding to, which means it keeps running on the days your motivation is gone, and those are the days that matter. So the entire craft of sustaining is to convert keeping from a decision you have to make into a habit you do not, and the way you do that is to make each keeping-act small.

This is the counterintuitive heart of it: lower the bar, deliberately, until the habit is almost impossible to fail. A one-minute reset of a single surface, done every day, will keep more of your home over a year than a two-hour blitz you manage twice and then dread. The small, dull, relentless version wins, every time, over the heroic version, because the small one actually keeps happening. And keeping is genuinely lighter than fixing: a home tended a little every day never gets bad enough to need the exhausting overhaul, so the household that sustains is not the one doing more work. It is the one that has quietly stopped doing the big, dreaded work at all.

The destinationUntil It Is Second Nature

Here is where all of this is heading, and it is worth holding in view, because it is the quiet promise the whole book has been walking toward.

Kept long enough, 6S stops being something you do to your home and becomes simply how your home is. That is the destination this whole book has been walking toward: not a home you are forever fixing, but one that mostly keeps itself, because keeping it has quietly become second nature.

There is a point, if you keep a home for long enough with small, shared habits, where the keeping stops feeling like a thing you are doing at all. Putting the keys on the hook is not a chore you remember to perform; it is just what your hand does. The after-dinner reset is not a routine anyone has to be reminded about; it is simply part of dinner, the way clearing your plate is. At that point the home is not being maintained by effort anymore. It is being maintained by identity, by the ordinary habits of the people who live there, and it stays good almost without anyone noticing they are keeping it. That is second nature, and it is not a fantasy. It is what any habit becomes once it has been small and consistent for long enough.

That is also the honest answer to a question you might have been carrying since the first chapter: does this ever get easier, or am I signing up to work on my house forever? It gets easier, genuinely and a great deal, but not because you finish. It gets easier because keeping becomes automatic, and automatic is nearly free. The effort curve of a well-kept home starts high, during the building, and then falls, year over year, toward almost nothing, not because the home stops needing care but because giving that care has stopped costing you anything to give. A home you keep on habit is not a burden you carry. It is a place that, quietly and permanently, holds you up.

Quick Win

Pick the smallest keeping-habit you could imagine actually doing forever, one minute, once a day, resetting a single surface, and start it today. Sustain is built from habits so small they survive your worst weeks, not from grand resolutions that die inside a month.

6S Tip

Lower the bar until the habit is unbreakable. A keeping-routine you do badly every day beats a perfect one you do for two weeks and abandon. Sustain rewards the small and relentless, never the heroic and brief.

The dialThe Needle Holds, and the Last Gap Appears

Go and look at the friction meter, because although it does not move this chapter, it shows you something it has never shown before.

The needle holds exactly where Standardize left it, at the mark, because a chapter about a mindset does not change a single thing in your rooms. But look at the small distance still remaining between the needle and the goal, the gap that has sat there, unexplained, since the very first chapter. For the first time, the dial names it: a faint dashed path runs from where the needle rests to the goal crosshair, and that path is Sustain.

You do not finish 6S. You keep it. The first five S's build a home worth keeping; the sixth is the habit of keeping it.

That last gap was never more clutter to clear or more friction to scrub away; the earlier S's already did all of that. It is the difference between a home that stays good because you are working at it and a home that stays good on its own, because keeping it has become second nature. You do not close that gap by pushing harder. You close it by letting the small habits run, month after month, year after year, until the effort of keeping fades toward nothing and the home simply holds. The catch that Standardize locked behind the needle keeps it from sliding back; Sustain is the slow, quiet walk the rest of the way to the goal, and it is completed not in this chapter but at the very end of the book, when 6S has become, for you, simply how a home is lived in.

Family Challenge

Talk about it as a household, once, and ask a bigger question than "can we keep this up?" Ask "how do we want to live now?" A home is kept by the people who live in it choosing to, together, not by one person quietly carrying it.

In closingSustain Has Only Begun

You have the mindset now, which is the thing this chapter came to give you: that a home is kept and not finished, that keeping runs on small shared habits rather than willpower, and that kept long enough it becomes second nature and nearly free. That mindset is the ground everything else in this last part stands on. What you do not yet have is the handful of concrete, ordinary practices that turn the mindset into a life, and those are the rest of Part Eight.

They are gentle and few. A light, regular way to check in on the home and catch drift early, before it becomes an overhaul, which is the next chapter and looks nothing like the inspection you might be dreading. A simple way for the whole household to solve the little problems a home throws up, together, instead of one person forever patching them alone. A small daily rhythm that folds keeping into the ordinary shape of a day. And a recurring event that resets and renews the whole thing, and carries you around the loop again, better each time. Those four, laid on top of the mindset you now hold, are what turn a good home into a home that stays good for as long as you live in it. For now, hold on to the one idea the whole sixth S rests on: you are not trying to finish. You are learning to keep.

Common Mistake

Treating 6S as a project you finished, so you stop, and then watching the whole thing quietly come undone over the following months. The moment you decide you are done is the moment the drift begins. You are never done. You are keeping.

One Idea to Keep

You do not finish 6S; you keep it. A home stays good the way a garden stays alive, by a little ongoing care from the people who love it, not by one heroic effort and then neglect. Sustain is that care, made small enough and shared enough to last for years.

Part Eight · Sustain

Chapter Twenty-Seven

6S Audits That Do Not Feel Like Inspections

The word audit makes everyone flinch, because it sounds like a test with an inspector and a grade. A home audit is the opposite: a quick, regular, friendly look at the house, not the people, to see what is still working and catch small drift before it grows. It checks the home, never the household, so a drift it finds is a system to fix, not a person to blame.

You have the mindset now, from the last chapter: that a home is kept rather than finished, on small shared habits, until keeping becomes second nature. That is the ground. This chapter lays the first stone on it, the first concrete, repeatable thing you actually do to keep the gains, and it is the humble, powerful practice of looking. A home holds its shape when someone, now and then, simply looks at it with clear eyes and notices what has begun to slip, while the slipping is still small and a two-minute matter.

The trouble is the name for this, which in 6S is the audit, and audit is a word that makes almost everyone tense up. It arrives carrying suitcases: tax inspectors, surprise checks, someone official with a clipboard deciding whether you passed, the cold feeling of being examined and found wanting. If that is what an audit meant for your home, I would tell you to skip it, because a household will not, and should not, submit itself to regular judgment, and any keeping-practice that feels like being put on trial is one that quietly gets abandoned within a month, with relief.

So the first and most important job of this chapter is to take that word apart and hand it back to you meaning something completely different. A home audit is not an inspection. It is a check-in: a quick, regular, warm look at the house, not the people, to see how the good things you built are holding up and to catch the small drift before it becomes a large mess. It is closer to feeling a child's forehead for a temperature than to a tax audit, an act of care rather than an act of judgment. Get that distinction right and the audit becomes something a whole household will happily do. Get it wrong and it dies on contact.

In this chapter

  • Understand why the word audit makes people flinch, and why a home audit is the opposite of an inspection.
  • Run a check-in: a quick, regular, friendly look at how the home is holding up.
  • Keep the audit on the home and never on the people, so a drift is a system to fix, not a person to blame.
  • Catch drift while it is small, when it is a two-minute fix rather than a lost weekend.
  • Keep the check-in short, regular, and owned, so it actually keeps happening.

The wordWhy "Audit" Makes Everyone Flinch

It is worth naming precisely what the word carries, because until you disarm it, everything else in this chapter will land wrong. When most people hear that they should audit their home, some part of them braces, as if they are about to be tested on it, and that bracing is the enemy.

An inspection is something done to people, to catch them out and grade them. A check-in is something done for a home, to see how it is holding up and help it early. It can be the same walk through the same rooms, and it will feel like the opposite thing, because one is looking for fault and the other is only looking for drift.

Read that carefully, because it holds the whole reframe. The mechanical act can be identical: someone walks through the house and looks at how things are. What changes everything is the orientation of the looking. An inspection points its attention at people and asks, in effect, who has failed to keep this up, so it produces defensiveness, hiding, and resentment, which is exactly why inspections make homes worse over time, not better. A check-in points its attention at the home and asks how the house is holding up, so it produces small, cheerful fixes and a household that does not mind at all. It is the difference between a doctor examining you kindly to keep you well and an examiner grading you to decide if you are good enough, and your body knows the difference the instant it walks in the room. Your family knows it too.

The hero ideaA Health Check for the House

So here, stated plainly and with the dread removed, is what you are actually doing.

What a home audit is

A 6S audit at home is a quick, regular, friendly walk through the house to see how the gains are holding up: what is still working, and where small drift has crept in, so you can fix it while it is small. It checks the home, not the people, and it is a health check, not a test.

That is the entire practice: a short, warm, regular look at the house. You already own an instrument for it, if you want one, in the simple snapshot you took right at the start to get your baseline; you can walk the same quick pass now, not to score where you began but to notice what has moved since. But the instrument matters far less than the spirit, and the spirit is captured in four small things that, between them, are the whole difference between an audit people run happily for years and one that dies after two tries.

What turns an inspection into a check-in: it looks at the home, not the people; it is light and quick; it is regular and expected; and it notices what is working, not only what has slipped.

Take those in turn, because each one defuses a different part of the dread. It looks at the home, not the people, so no one is on trial. It is light and quick, a few minutes and not a formal reckoning, so it never becomes a burden anyone avoids. It is regular and expected, part of the ordinary rhythm rather than a surprise sprung on the household, so it carries no ambush and no fear. And it notices what is working, not only what has slipped, so it feels like appreciation as much as correction, and people leave it encouraged rather than scolded. Miss any one of these and the audit tips back toward inspection; hold all four and it becomes what it should be, an easy, welcome habit of care.

The no-blame moveLook at the Home, Not the Household

Of those four, the first is the one everything else hangs on, and it is worth its own moment, because it is where good intentions most often go wrong. The whole practice lives or dies on keeping the attention on the room and off the roommate.

The moment an audit becomes about who let the shelf slip, it dies, because nobody volunteers to be inspected. Keep it about the shelf. A shelf that drifted is not a failure of anyone's character; it is a small system that needs a small adjustment, and the audit's only job is to find it kindly and set it right.

This is not soft-heartedness; it is what actually works. The instant an audit starts assigning blame, two things happen, and both of them wreck it. First, people become defensive, and a defensive household stops being honest about drift, so the audit loses the very information it exists to gather. Second, and worse, people learn the real lesson you are teaching, which is that mess is punished, and they respond the way anyone responds to that: not by keeping the home better, but by hiding the mess before audit day and putting on a show of order for the inspection. You will have trained your family to fake a clean house on a schedule, which is precisely the opposite of what you wanted. Keep it about the shelf and none of that happens. A drifted shelf is a neutral fact about a system, like a low tyre, and you simply top it up. The blamelessness is not a nicety. It is the thing that keeps the audit honest and therefore useful.

Timing and lightnessCatch It Early, Keep It Light

The last thing to understand is why you do this regularly and keep it small, and the answer is entirely about timing, because in a home the cost of a problem depends almost completely on how long it has been left.

The whole value of a regular check-in is timing. A drift caught this week is a two-minute fix; the same drift caught in six months is a lost weekend. You do not audit the home to judge it. You audit it so that it never again has to be rescued.

Drift compounds. One thing left in the wrong place invites a second, because a surface that is already a little cluttered signals that clutter is allowed here; a system used slightly wrong a few times quietly becomes used wrong by default. Caught in its first week, almost any drift is a shrug and a small correction. Left for half a year, the same drift has recruited friends and hardened into the new normal, and undoing it is a whole dreaded project of the kind Sustain exists to make unnecessary. So you look often and lightly, because a five-minute check every week or two catches drift while it is still trivial, and a household that does that never again meets the exhausting, morale-crushing overhaul. And keep it genuinely light, because only the light version survives: a short, low-key walk that people can actually do forever beats a thorough, solemn reckoning that they manage twice and then avoid. If you want, let each person check their own zone rather than one person checking everyone's, which turns the whole thing from being inspected into taking quiet pride in your own patch, and people are remarkably honest about their own drift when nobody is standing over them with a pen.

Quick Win

Do one two-minute audit right now. Walk a single room and ask, of the room and not of anyone in it, "what has drifted since we set this up?" Fix the first small thing you find. That is a whole audit, and it was not frightening at all.

6S Tip

Keep it short and regular. A five-minute check every week catches far more than a two-hour reckoning once a year, and only the short one actually keeps happening. You can reuse the simple snapshot from your baseline audit; you do not need a new instrument.

The dialThe Needle Takes Its First Sustain Step

Go and look at the friction meter, because it moves again, just a little, and it is the first movement since Standardize.

Last chapter the needle held, and the dial revealed the last small gap to the goal as a dashed path. This chapter you have laid down the first real piece of keeping-machinery, a regular, kindly check-in, and so the needle takes its first Sustain step, a short move along that dashed path. It is a small step, and honestly so, because an audit does not clear a single thing on its own; it scrubs no surface and removes no clutter. What it does is subtler and, over years, larger: it makes the home a little more able to keep itself, because drift is now met while it is small instead of discovered when it is large, and a home that catches its own drift early is a home that needs less minding to stay good.

An audit checks the home, not the household. What it finds is always a system to fix, never a person to blame.

That is why the move is real even though nothing was cleared today. The gap between the needle and the goal is shorter now, and the dashed remainder is the rest of the distance the next chapters close: solving the recurring problems the audit keeps finding, folding the keeping into the daily rhythm, and coming back around, every so often, for a full renewal. The catch that Standardize locked behind the needle still holds it against sliding back; the audit is the first of the small, steady pushes that walk it the rest of the way to the goal.

Family Challenge

Let each person check their own zone rather than one person checking everyone's. A self-audit you own beats an inspection you resent, and people turn out to be honest about their own drift when nobody is grading them.

In closingKeeping Has Begun

You have taken the first real step of keeping. You started with the mindset, that a home is kept and not finished, and now you have the first practice that puts it to work: a regular, friendly check-in that looks at the home, catches drift while it is small, and never once puts the household on trial. Run kindly and often, that single habit will spare you more dreaded overhauls than any amount of heroic cleaning, because it means your home never again gets far enough from good to need rescuing.

What the audit does not do, by design, is solve the bigger things it finds. A check-in is brilliant at catching drift and fixing the small stuff on the spot, but every so often it will turn up a real, recurring problem, the same thing drifting in the same place month after month, which no amount of quick correction will settle because the system itself is wrong. Fixing those, together, as a household, instead of one person forever patching them alone, is a practice of its own, and it is the next chapter. Past that lies folding the keeping into the ordinary shape of a day, and then the recurring event that renews the whole thing and completes the book. For now, hold the one idea this chapter turns on: an audit is a kindness you do for your home, not a judgment you pass on your family.

Common Mistake

Turning the audit into a performance review of the people, with scores held over someone's head. The instant it feels like judgment, everyone starts hiding the mess before the audit instead of fixing it, and you have taught the household to fake a clean home for inspection day. Check the home, kindly, and never the person.

One Idea to Keep

Keep the gains with a light, regular check-in that looks at the home and never at the people. A drift caught small is a small fix; a drift left to grow is an overhaul. Audit the house kindly and often, and it will never again need rescuing.

The next chapter gives the whole household a simple, shared way to solve those, together, instead of one person forever patching them alone.

↑ Contents

Part Eight · Sustain

Chapter Twenty-Eight

Family Problem Solving

Some drift is not a slip to correct but a signal that a small system is wrong, and quick fixes will never settle it, because you keep patching the symptom while the cause sits untouched. When the same problem keeps coming back, the household stops patching and solves it together: by asking why it happens, never who is to blame, and changing the little system so it cannot easily happen again.

If you have started running the friendly check-in from the last chapter, you have probably noticed that most of what it turns up is easy: a small drift, a two-minute correction, done and forgotten. But you will also have noticed a different, more stubborn kind of finding, the one that shows up on the check-in this week, and last week, and the week before. The same coats on the same chair. The same dishes stacking by the sink instead of going in. The same shoes blocking the same doorway. You keep fixing them, and they keep coming back, and a small, tired frustration begins to build, because it feels like the home, or the family, or you, keeps failing at something simple.

Here is the reframe that dissolves that frustration, and it is the whole of this chapter. A problem that keeps coming back is not a slip anyone is failing to correct. It is a signal that a small system is wrong. The coats return to the chair not because your household lacks discipline but because something about the setup quietly makes the chair the easiest place to put them. And a wrong system cannot be fixed by correcting it more often, any more than a leaking pipe can be fixed by mopping the floor more diligently. It has to be solved, at the cause, once.

That is a different skill from everything the book has taught so far, and it is the last one Sustain needs. It is the ability, as a household, to take one of those recurring problems, understand why it really keeps happening, and change the little system so that it stops, for good. And the two things that make it work, more than any technique, are these: you ask why it happens and never who is to blame, and you solve it together, as the people who actually live with it. Get those two right and the exhausting loop of fixing the same thing forever simply ends.

In this chapter

  • Tell a one-off slip from a recurring problem, and treat the two completely differently.
  • Stop patching the symptom, and solve the cause instead.
  • Ask why a problem keeps happening, not who keeps causing it, until you reach the real cause.
  • See the real cause as a design flaw in a small system, never a character flaw in a person.
  • Solve the problem together, so the household owns the fix and actually keeps it.

The core distinctionFixing Is Not Solving

Start with the distinction the whole chapter turns on, because naming it changes how you feel the moment a problem returns.

A problem you have to fix more than twice is not a problem you are failing to fix. It is a problem you are failing to solve. Fixing puts the thing back; solving changes why it fell in the first place, so that you never have to put it back again.

These are two genuinely different activities, and we confuse them constantly, to our exhaustion. Fixing is correcting the symptom: the coats are on the chair, so you hang them up. It is necessary, it is quick, and it is completely temporary, because it does nothing about whatever put the coats there, which is still fully in place and will do it again tonight. Solving is different: it looks past the symptom to the cause and changes that, so the symptom stops being produced. Fixing is mopping the floor; solving is finding the leak. Both have their place, and mopping is right for a spill, but if you find yourself mopping the same square of floor every single day, some part of you already knows that more mopping is not the answer. The recurring problems your check-in keeps surfacing are exactly that same square of floor, and this chapter is about finally looking up to find the pipe.

What family problem solving is

Family problem solving is how a household settles the recurring problems a home throws up, together: when the same thing keeps drifting back, you stop patching the symptom, ask why it keeps happening rather than who is to blame, and change the small system so it cannot easily happen again. It fixes the cause once, instead of the symptom forever.

The method's heartAsk Why, Not Who

The tool for finding the cause is embarrassingly simple, and it hinges entirely on asking the right question, because the wrong question sends you in exactly the wrong direction.

When something keeps going wrong, the useless question is who keeps doing it, and the useful one is why it keeps happening. Who finds a person to blame and changes nothing; why finds a system to fix and changes everything. The coats are not on the chair because someone is lazy. They are on the chair because the hooks are in the wrong place.

This carries forward, straight into problem-solving, the no-blame spirit you learned to give the audit, and it matters even more here. Ask "who keeps dumping their coat on the chair", and you get a defensive family member, a small argument, and a coat that is back on the chair tomorrow, because you have identified a culprit but changed nothing about the situation that produced the behaviour. Ask "why do the coats keep landing on the chair", and you are suddenly looking at the real thing: the chair is right by the door, the coat hooks are down the hall in a closet, and every tired person coming home does the sensible, path-of-least-resistance thing and drops the coat on the nearest surface. Nobody is failing. The system is simply asking people to walk further than a tired human will walk, and it loses that argument every time.

The way you get from the symptom to that cause is just to keep gently asking why, a few times over, the way a curious child would. Why are the coats on the chair? Because it is the easiest place. Why is it the easiest place? Because the hooks are far away. Why does that matter so much? Because people are tired when they come in and will always take the shortest path. A few whys in, you have walked from a symptom you were blaming a person for to a cause you can actually change, and you will notice something reassuring along the way: the real cause is almost always a design flaw, not a character flaw. It is a missing hook, an awkward distance, a bin that is too far, a shelf with no label, a thing with no home. That is genuinely good news, because you cannot easily change a person, but you can nearly always change a system.

OwnershipSolve It Together

There is one more thing that decides whether a solution survives, and it is not how clever the solution is. It is who came up with it.

The person who lives with a problem is the one who knows why it really happens, and the one who has to keep any fix alive, so they are exactly who should help design it. A solution handed down is resented and quietly dropped; a solution the household worked out together is one it actually keeps.

You met this principle when you assigned the standards a few chapters back: what is chosen gets done, and what is imposed gets subverted. It is doubly true for problem-solving, for two reasons. The first is knowledge: the person who actually lives with the problem, the teenager whose bag always ends up in the hall, the parent who always finds the dishes by the sink, knows things about why it happens that you, solving it from the outside, simply do not. They know the real friction, the reason the obvious fix would not work, the small thing that would. Leave them out and you will design a worse solution. The second is ownership: any fix, however good, needs the people around it to keep using it, and people keep what they helped build and abandon what was dropped on them from above. So you bring the recurring problem to the household, out loud, as a shared puzzle rather than a verdict, and you let everyone, including the children, who are often startlingly good at this, propose the fix. The solution you land on together will be better than the one you would have imposed, and, far more importantly, it will still be running in a month.

The method in actionA Worked Problem

Let me put the whole thing together on the coats, because seeing it run once is worth more than any amount of description. The method is just four small steps, done together.

Solve a recurring problem together in four small steps: name the problem that keeps drifting back; ask why, a few times, until you reach the real cause; change the small system so the cause is gone; and let the people who live with it help decide the fix, so they keep it.

The check-in keeps flagging the same thing: coats on the chair by the door, every week. So instead of hanging them up a two-hundredth time, the household sits down for five minutes and does four small things. First, they name the problem plainly, as a problem and not a person: the coats keep ending up on the chair. Second, they ask why, together, a few times, and arrive not at a guilty party but at a cause everyone recognizes the moment it is said: the hooks are down the hall, the chair is right there, and tired people take the shortest path. Third, they change the small system to remove that cause: a row of hooks goes up on the wall right beside the door, so now the shortest path and the right path are the same path. And fourth, because the whole family worked it out and one of the kids picked where the hooks went and got to hammer one in, it is theirs, and they use it. The coats go on the hooks, the chair stays clear, and the problem that returned every week for a year quietly stops returning at all. That is the entire method, and it works on almost anything: the dishes, the shoes, the homework, the endless small recurring frictions of a shared home.

Quick Win

Take the one thing in your home you are tired of fixing, the pile that always returns to the same spot, and ask out loud, "why does this keep happening here?", three or four times, until you reach something you can actually change. You just started solving it instead of fixing it.

6S Tip

The real cause is almost always a design flaw, not a character flaw: the bin is too far, the hook is too high, the shelf has no label, the thing has no home. When a problem keeps returning, look for the missing or awkward part of the system before you look at the people.

The dialThe Needle Takes Its Second Sustain Step

Go and look at the friction meter, because it moves again, a little further along the path it revealed two chapters ago.

Last chapter, the audit took the needle its first Sustain step, by helping the home catch drift while it was small. This chapter goes a level deeper: instead of catching the same drift faster, you have stopped it from returning at all, by solving the system behind it. So the needle takes its second Sustain step, a little further toward the goal. It is small, honestly so, because you solved one recurring problem, not all of them at once; but it is real, because solving a recurring problem changes something permanent. A source of friction that used to come back every single week is simply gone now, and it is not coming back, and a home with one fewer returning problem is a home that keeps itself that little bit more on its own.

When the same problem keeps coming back, stop fixing it and start solving it: ask why it happens, not who is to blame, and change the system so it cannot easily happen again.

That is the shape of the whole Sustain endgame, and you can see it on the dial now: not one big leap, but a series of small, permanent gains, each one making the home a touch more self-tending, walking the needle steadily down the last stretch toward the goal. The catch that Standardize locked still holds everything against sliding back; the audit catches what drifts; and now problem-solving removes what keeps drifting, at the source. The dashed remainder of the path is shorter again, and the final two chapters close it.

Family Challenge

Bring one recurring annoyance to the whole household, phrase it as "why does this keep happening?" and never "who keeps doing this?", and let everyone, including the children, propose a fix. The best solution often comes from the very person you were about to blame.

In closingKeeping Grows

Look at what keeping has become. You started with a mindset, that a home is kept and not finished. You added a check-in that catches drift while it is small. And now you have a way to take the drift that keeps returning and end it at the source, together, without anyone being blamed. Those three, held together, are most of what it takes to keep a home good for years: you notice early, and you solve what recurs, so the home neither slides back all at once nor wears you down with the same small battles fought over and over.

Two things remain, and both are about rhythm rather than technique. The first is folding all of this keeping into the ordinary shape of a day, so that the small acts of upkeep happen at natural, set moments instead of relying on anyone remembering to do them; that is the next chapter. The second is coming back around, every so often, for a full renewal, the recurring event that carries you through the whole loop again, better each time, and completes the book. For now, hold the one idea this chapter turns on: when something keeps going wrong, do not look for someone to blame. Look, together, for the small system to fix.

Common Mistake

Solving the problem for the family instead of with them, by imposing a clever fix nobody asked for. However good it is, it will be resented and abandoned within a fortnight, because people keep what they helped build and drop what was dropped on them. Solve it together, or do not bother.

One Idea to Keep

When the same problem keeps coming back, stop fixing it and start solving it. Ask why it keeps happening, together, not who is to blame, until you reach the real cause, then change the small system so it cannot easily happen again. Fix the cause once, and you will never fix the symptom again.
